Project Phase: Week 6 - HealthConnect Rwanda: Healthcare Analytics & Predictive Modeling Project

Project Overview¶

This notebook serves as the comprehensive data science environment for the HealthConnect Rwanda Healthcare Analytics and Artificial Intelligence Transformation Project (Path 2: Healthcare Predictive Analytics and Population Health Intelligence).

HealthConnect Rwanda manages a vast ecosystem of clinical, operational, financial, and administrative data across 30 logical tables assembled from CSV files and multi-sheet Excel workbooks. This project aims to extract actionable insights, build predictive models for patient admissions and hospital revenues, perform advanced data cleaning, and formulate strategic recommendations to optimize healthcare delivery and resource allocation.

Notebook Structure¶

  • Part 1: Data Acquisition, Structural Understanding & Entity Relationship Modeling (ERD)
  • Part 2: Data Cleaning & Preprocessing
  • Part 3: Data Validation & Quality Assessment
  • Part 4: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
  • Part 5: Feature Engineering
  • Part 6: Statistical Analysis & Hypothesis Testing
  • Part 7: Predictive Analytics, Forecasting & Clustering
  • Part 8: Business Insights & Strategic Recommendations

Part 1: Data Acquisition & Structural Understanding¶

In this first section, we ingest all logical datasets provided by HealthConnect Rwanda, including CSV files and multi-sheet Excel workbooks. We inspect their dimensions, data types, and structural integrity. Following ingestion, we utilize Graphviz to construct and visualize an Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD), mapping the primary and foreign key relationships across tables to establish a clear structural foundation for subsequent analytical modeling.

Part 2: Data Cleaning & Preprocessing¶

2.1 - Data Integration at the Appointment Grain¶

Integration principle¶

The source tables describe different entities and have different levels of detail. A direct join of every table would multiply appointment rows when an appointment has several diagnoses, tests, prescriptions, bills, payments, or feedback records. The analytical master table will therefore use one row per appointment. One-to-many clinical and financial tables will be summarized to appointment level before they are joined.

The original relational tables remain available in datasets for traceability. Cleaning is applied to the integrated appointment-level master table used in the downstream analysis. The master table excludes direct patient identifiers such as names, phone numbers, and emergency contacts. Source-level duplicate copies are combined during ingestion; exact repeated rows are removed, while distinct records are retained for quality review.

2.3 - Master DataFrame Cleaning and Preprocessing¶

The cleaning target is the integrated, appointment-level master_df, which is the analytical dataset used in the next parts of this notebook. The source tables are retained unchanged in datasets for traceability and for later domain-specific analyses; they are not separately exported as cleaned datasets.

Missingness is interpreted by field meaning. Absence of a related event is represented with a zero count or an explicit No record label. A missing chronic-condition value is labelled Not recorded, because the source does not prove that the patient has no condition. Appointments without feedback receive the Not rated satisfaction category; their scores are not fabricated. Required identifiers and dates are validated rather than imputed. The cleaned master should have no null values, while explicit labels preserve what was not observed.

2.4 - Data Quality Report: Scope and Cleaning Evidence¶

The pre-clean audit profiles the supplied logical tables and validates the available primary-key and foreign-key relationships. The cleaning log applies corrections only to the integrated appointment-level master table. The original source tables are retained unchanged in datasets so the source values remain traceable.

The post-clean summary must show zero null cells and unique appointmentid values in master_df_clean. A zero-null master does not mean every source value was observed: labels such as Not recorded, No record, and Not rated preserve that distinction. Numeric satisfaction ratings remain in the original Patient_Feedback table and should be used only for appointments with observed feedback. Facility foreign keys remain not independently verifiable because the supplied project data has no facility master table.

Part 3: Data Validation & Quality Assessment¶

Part 2 profiled the source tables and cleaned the appointment-level master. This section independently validates the resulting analytical dataset and checks key relationships against source tables. It separates structural failures from findings requiring source-owner review, so inconsistencies are not silently interpreted as valid business facts.

3.1 - Structural, Referential, and Domain Validation¶

The checks verify the one-row-per-appointment grain, key uniqueness, completeness after cleaning, expected identifier coverage, value domains, and financial non-negativity. Department-to-facility mapping and billing-status/payment inconsistencies are reported for review, not automatically corrected. Events outside the appointment cohort are counted separately because they may belong to a wider extract rather than represent broken keys.

Interpretation & Validation Findings¶

  • Master structure: There are 5,000 rows for 5,000 unique appointments and no residual null cells after cleaning. Explicit labels such as Not recorded, No record, and Not rated still preserve missing-source meaning.
  • Core relationships: Patient, doctor, and department identifiers match their available parent tables, and the appointment ID set agrees with the source. The selected appointment grain is intact.
  • Department/facility mapping requires review: 4,744 of 5,000 appointments (94.9%) have a FacilityID that differs from the FacilityID listed for the same DepartmentID in Departments. Both source values remain unchanged. Facility-level attribution should be treated cautiously until the mapping is reconciled.
  • Billing status conflicts with transactions: Paid bills retain calculated balances, while Pending bills also have linked payments. The transaction amounts are used for receipt and balance calculations; the status labels remain findings for source-owner review.
  • Out-of-cohort events: The scope table counts child records linked to the 5,000 appointments and those outside the cohort. Out-of-cohort records are excluded from appointment-level analyses, but are not automatically called invalid because they may belong to a wider extract.
  • Validation result: Structural checks, core keys, age range, and non-negative amounts pass. Department/facility alignment and billing status/payment alignment remain review findings.

Part 4: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

This part explores patient profiles, clinical activity, operational capacity, financial performance, and patient experience using the cleaned appointment-level master table. Detailed event tables are restricted to appointment identifiers present in master_df_clean before analysis. Each chart is titled and labeled, and its interpretation highlights both the observed pattern and relevant data limitations.

4.1 - Patient Analysis¶

This section describes the demographic and health profile of patients represented in the appointment cohort. Patient growth is measured as first observed appointments by month because the source data do not provide a patient registration date. Geographic results are summarized by administrative area; map boundaries and coordinates are not supplied.

Appointment cohort: 5,000 appointments; 4,443 distinct patients.
Age summary (years), one row per patient:

age 4443.0 45.517893 26.149465 0.0 23.0 46.0 68.0 90.0 
Patients with a recorded chronic condition: 3,312 / 4,443 (74.5%); missing condition history is excluded from this prevalence estimate.

Interpretation & Patient Insights - Visuals 1 to 7¶

  • Visual 1 (Gender Distribution): The 4,443 distinct patients are almost evenly divided: 2,256 male (50.8%) and 2,187 female (49.2%). The difference is only 69 patients, so neither gender dominates this appointment cohort.
  • Visual 2 (Age Distribution): The histogram spans ages 0 to 90 rather than concentrating in one narrow age band. The median is 46 years, the mean is 45.5, and the middle half of patients falls between 23 and 68 years. This indicates that the service cohort includes children and older adults as well as working-age patients; the chart describes patients with appointments, not Rwanda's age structure.
  • Visual 3 (Blood Group Distribution): Counts are fairly close across the seven recorded blood groups, from 591 for O- to 653 for A-. The 62-patient spread is small relative to the cohort, so there is no single blood group that dominates the recorded patient profile.
  • Visual 4 (Insurance ID Availability): All 4,443 distinct patients have an InsuranceID recorded, which is why the chart has one bar. This confirms identifier completeness in the selected cohort only. There is no insurance-status or insurer lookup table here, so the chart cannot establish active coverage, eligibility, or benefit level.
  • Visual 5 (Recorded Chronic Conditions): Among patients with a recorded condition, counts are similar: Asthma 1,116, Hypertension 1,104, and Diabetes 1,092. However, 1,131 patients (25.5%) have no recorded chronic-condition history. The three condition counts must therefore be read as recorded categories, not confirmed prevalence; missing history may change their true proportions.
  • Visual 6 (Geographic Distribution by Province): Western has the largest cohort count (930; 20.9%) and Kigali City the smallest (850; 19.1%). The 80-patient gap across the five provinces suggests broadly even representation in these records. Because no provincial population denominators are available, this is not a comparison of healthcare access or population-level rates.
  • Visual 7 (Patients First Observed by Month): The series peaks in March at 419 first-observed patients and reaches its low in December at 311, a 25.8% difference from the March peak. Counts generally ease after March, with a temporary rebound in June (403). Since there is no patient registration date, this is only the first appointment date observed in the supplied data; it should not be described as actual patient growth or a confirmed seasonal pattern.

4.2 - Clinical Analysis¶

Clinical event tables can contain records outside the appointment cohort and may contain multiple rows per appointment. The analyses below first keep only events linked to the cleaned master appointment identifiers, then count events or appointments according to the chart’s stated unit. Severity is descriptive and is not treated as a validated clinical outcome.

Cohort-filtered clinical record counts:
Diagnoses: 5,000 rows
Laboratory_Tests: 2,272 rows
Prescriptions: 4,003 rows
Admissions: 586 rows
Referrals: 415 rows

Interpretation & Clinical Insights - Visuals 8 to 13¶

  • Visual 8 (Diagnosis Frequency): All 5,000 cohort appointments have a linked diagnosis. The five diagnoses occur in a relatively narrow range: Hypertension leads with 1,059 (21.2%), followed by Gastritis 1,017 (20.3%), Upper Respiratory Infection 1,004 (20.1%), Diabetes 985 (19.7%), and Malaria 935 (18.7%). No diagnosis overwhelms the distribution. These frequencies describe the records provided, not disease incidence in the wider population.
  • Visual 9 (Laboratory Test Utilization): Laboratory records are linked to 2,272 appointments, or 45.4% of the 5,000-appointment cohort. The four test categories are also quite balanced: Malaria 591 (26.0%), CBC 583 (25.7%), Glucose 560 (24.6%), and Urinalysis 538 (23.7%) of linked test records. The bar chart counts test records, not test results, abnormal findings, or clinical necessity.
  • Visual 10 (Prescription Frequency): Prescriptions appear for 4,003 appointments (80.1%). Amlodipine is the most frequent medication (851; 21.3% of prescription records) and Artemether-Lumefantrine the least frequent among the listed top categories (738; 18.4%). The close spacing indicates no one medication dominates this dataset. Counts do not measure dosage, adherence, treatment success, or appropriateness.
  • Visual 11 (Diagnosis Severity): Moderate (1,696; 33.9%), Mild (1,682; 33.6%), and Severe (1,622; 32.4%) labels are nearly evenly represented. The small difference between the largest and smallest categories is 74 records. This balance may reflect how the source data were generated or recorded; severity labels have not been clinically validated.
  • Visual 12 (Admission-Linked Appointments by Month): The chart counts distinct appointments with an admission record. Monthly counts range from 35 in August to 61 in July, with a noticeable July-to-August drop and a rebound to 52 in October and 56 in November. The variation does not form a steady upward or downward trend. This is not a count of admission days or bed occupancy.
  • Visual 13 (Referral-Linked Appointments by Month): Referral-linked appointments range from 30 in October to 42 in March. The monthly line fluctuates, with a March peak (42) and a second-highest month in August (40); it does not show a sustained trend. The source only records referral linkage, so the chart says nothing about referral completion or destination outcomes.

Cohort scope: Clinical tables were filtered to the 5,000 AppointmentIDs in master_df_clean; unmatched source records are intentionally excluded from these cohort charts.

4.3 - Operational Analysis¶

Operational indicators are calculated from appointment volume and staff or equipment rosters. The available files do not assign nurses to individual appointments, provide bed occupancy events, or identify equipment usage; therefore, roster counts and appointment volumes are used as operational context rather than measured workload or utilization rates.

Listed beds: 2,000; source status values: {'Available': 2000}

Interpretation & Operational Insights - Visuals 14 to 19¶

  • Visual 14 (Appointments by Doctor): The 12 highest-volume doctors each have between 22 and 28 appointments in this cohort; the leading doctor has 28. Across all 350 listed doctors the mean is 14.3 cohort appointments, with a range of 5 to 28. This shows variation in observed appointment counts, but no shift length, working hours, specialty case mix, or assignment history is available to determine whether the difference represents workload imbalance.
  • Visual 15 (Listed Nurses by Department): The departments at the top of the roster chart are tied at four listed nurses. In the full roster, departments have either three or four nurses, so staffing counts are unusually uniform. The chart describes roster distribution only; it does not measure how many patients each nurse served.
  • Visual 16 (Appointment Volume by Facility): Among the 12 facilities shown, volumes range from 243 at HF017 to 278 at HF013, a spread of 35 appointments. The top facilities are therefore fairly close in absolute appointment counts. The chart omits the other eight facilities and has no capacity denominator, so these counts cannot be read as facility utilization rates.
  • Visual 17 (Bed Roster Status): All 2,000 listed beds are labeled Available. A single status category contains no variation and should be interpreted as a roster snapshot or source label, not evidence that every bed was unoccupied throughout the year. There is no admission-to-bed link or dated occupancy history.
  • Visual 18 (Equipment Distribution by Department): The plotted departments each have one equipment record; across the source roster, all 200 departments have exactly one record. The even pattern likely reflects the way this roster was assembled. Equipment counts do not show whether items are functional, available, or used.
  • Visual 19 (Patients per Listed Staff by Department): The plotted ratios differ across departments because patient counts and roster counts differ, and some departments have small staff denominators. These are crude patients-to-roster comparisons, not assigned patient panels or actual doctor/nurse workload. They should not be used to rank staffing adequacy without staff assignments, shifts, and department capacity data.

4.4 - Financial Analysis¶

The unlinked monthly Revenue_Summary table cannot be joined to appointments, departments, or patients. For linked financial analyses, billing records are connected through AppointmentID, payments and insurance claims through BillingID, and all records are restricted to the master appointment cohort. Payment amounts represent recorded receipts; invoice amounts and outstanding balances are reported separately.

Cohort billing records: 5,000; linked claims: 3,521.
Billed amount: 771,133,439.00; recorded payments: 694,551,320.00; calculated outstanding balance: 76,582,119.00.
The standalone Revenue_Summary is kept separate for later reconciliation; it is not allocated across departments.

Interpretation & Financial Insights - Visuals 20 to 25¶

  • Visual 20 (Monthly Billed Amounts and Recorded Receipts): Billed totals range from 57.2 million in September to 70.2 million in June; linked receipts range from 51.4 million in September to 62.9 million in June. The two lines move in broadly similar directions, and receipts remain below billed amounts in each month. This is a descriptive comparison in source amount units; currency is not specified, and the separate Revenue_Summary is not used in this chart.
  • Visual 21 (Billing Distribution by Status): The 5,000 billing records are split fairly evenly: 1,689 Partially Paid, 1,685 Paid, and 1,626 Pending. The differences are small, so status labels do not reveal a dominant billing state. The next chart comparison is important because the status and payment data are not internally consistent.
  • Visual 22 (Insurance Claims by Status): The cohort contains 3,521 linked claims: 1,774 Approved and 1,747 Pending. The counts are nearly equal, so approval is not the dominant state in these records. Claim status and claim amount should not be equated with cash received; claims are a separate process linked through BillingID.
  • Visual 23 (Calculated Outstanding Balance by Billing Status): Calculated balances are similar across the three statuses, from 24.9 million for Paid to 26.4 million for Pending. This is counterintuitive: Paid records still have balances, while Pending records also have large linked payment totals. The plot therefore exposes a status-versus-transaction inconsistency rather than a trustworthy status-based aging profile. Balances use max(Amount - matched AmountPaid, 0) per bill.
  • Visual 24 (Recorded Payment Amounts by Method): Receipts are spread fairly evenly across Card (177.9 million), Insurance (175.4 million), Cash (171.3 million), and Mobile Money (170.0 million). The 7.9 million difference between the largest and smallest method is modest relative to total receipts; no channel clearly dominates. These totals are transaction amounts, not payment counts or customer preferences.
  • Visual 25 (Recorded Receipts by Department): Cardiology leads the departments shown at 78.2 million, followed by Radiology at 73.6 million and Pediatrics at 71.1 million; the next departments are close behind. This attributes matched payment records to the appointment department. It is not directly comparable with the standalone monthly Revenue_Summary, which has no join key and may use a different scope or revenue definition.

Financial control implication: Do not infer collections or receivables from Billing.Status alone until the source owner reconciles those labels to payment transactions.

4.5 - Patient Experience¶

Patient experience is assessed from feedback records linked to the appointment cohort. The analysis reports rating distributions and feedback patterns by month, department, and facility. Feedback coverage is not assumed to represent all patients, and comments are not interpreted as a validated sentiment score.

Interpretation & Patient Experience Insights - Visuals 26 to 29¶

  • Visual 26 (Satisfaction Rating Distribution): The mode is 3 stars (387 records), followed by 1 star (366), 2 stars (353), 4 stars (346), and 5 stars (304). Ratings are spread across the full scale rather than concentrated at 4-5. In total, 719 responses (40.9%) are ratings 1-2, compared with 650 (37.0%) ratings 4-5; the overall mean is 2.93 and median is 3. This suggests mixed feedback with a slightly larger low-rating share, not uniformly positive experience.
  • Visual 27 (Feedback Volume by Month): Monthly response counts fluctuate between 132 and 165. October has the most feedback (165) and April the least (132); March is also high at 164. The line shows changing response volume, not a satisfaction trend. Monthly average scores range from 2.82 in September to 3.06 in January and move up and down rather than improving consistently.
  • Visual 28 (Average Rating by Department): Department averages run from 2.76 in ICU (172 responses) to 3.02 in Emergency (186 responses), a difference of 0.26 on a five-point scale. The departments cluster near three stars; this is a modest separation, not evidence by itself of a major service-quality gap. The response counts are substantial but do not eliminate non-response bias.
  • Visual 29 (Facility Rating Comparison): The revised chart compares the six lowest and six highest facility averages and labels each with its response count. HF020 is lowest at 2.76 (82 ratings), while HF011 is highest at 3.19 (91 ratings). The visible 0.43-point gap is worth investigating, but facility averages are descriptive and may reflect different patient mix or response patterns; they are not adjusted performance scores.

Coverage caveat: Feedback is linked to 1,756 of 5,000 appointments (35.1%). The results summarize submitted feedback and may not represent patients who did not respond.

4.6 - Visualization and Multivariate Review¶

The domain sections above provide histograms, bar charts, and time-series lines. This final review adds a correlation heatmap, a pair plot, a density plot, and a scatter plot for selected numeric fields. Geographic bar charts are used where location labels exist; a true geographic map requires coordinates or boundary geometry that is not part of the provided files.

Selected numeric variables: ['age', 'bmi', 'heightcm', 'weightkg', 'doctoryearsexperience', 'diagnoses_record_count', 'laboratory_tests_record_count', 'prescriptions_record_count', 'total_lengthofstay_days', 'total_billed_amount', 'total_amount_paid', 'total_claim_amount']
Correlation values are descriptive associations and do not imply causality.

Interpretation & Multivariate Insights - Visuals 30 to 35¶

  • Visual 30 (Correlation Heatmap): The strongest positive relationships are between BMI and weight (r = 0.84), and between billed amount and paid amount (r = 0.91). BMI and height show a negative association (r = -0.52), which is unexpected for a cohort where BMI is derived from height and weight and deserves a source-formula/data validation check. Billed amount and total claim amount have a moderate positive association (r = 0.56). Most age, clinical-event-count, and length-of-stay correlations with the other fields are close to zero. These are linear associations among appointment-level columns; aggregated financial totals share the same billing/payment process, so their high correlation is not independent evidence of causation.
  • Visual 31 (Pair Plot): The diagonal panels show the distributions of age, BMI, billed amount, and paid amount; the off-diagonal panels show their pairwise scatter. Age has little visible linear separation from BMI or financial totals. Billed and paid amounts rise together, consistent with the heatmap, but the points do not lie on a single one-to-one line, reflecting partial payments and other transaction differences. The plot uses an 800-row sample for readability and is descriptive, not an inferential test.
  • Visual 32 (Age Density): The density curve covers a broad age range rather than forming a narrow, bell-shaped peak. There are mild variations in density across age bands, but no single age band accounts for most of the patient cohort. KDE smoothing can make local peaks appear more pronounced; the histogram and summary statistics should be used together.
  • Visual 33 (Age Box Plot by Gender): Median age is 45 for males and 46 for females, and the interquartile ranges are almost identical (approximately 23-68 and 24-69). The boxes and whiskers overlap heavily, so this cohort shows no material age-profile separation by gender.
  • Visual 34 (BMI Violin Plot by Gender): BMI distributions overlap closely. Female median BMI is 28.9 (IQR 21.8-36.9) and male median is 29.4 (IQR 21.7-37.3). The similar medians and quartiles suggest little difference in the central BMI distribution between genders; the violin width indicates where observations are more concentrated, not a confidence interval.
  • Visual 35 (Age vs. BMI Scatter Plot): Points are widely spread vertically across nearly all ages, with no obvious linear slope. Similar BMI values occur at younger and older ages, which agrees with the near-zero age-BMI correlation. This does not rule out nonlinear relationships or clinical effects after adjusting for other factors.

Reading these figures together: The demographic charts count one row per distinct patient, while most heatmap and pair-plot fields are appointment-level aggregates. Repeat appointments and constructed totals can affect apparent associations. Correlation and visual overlap do not establish causality.

This part creates the ten features requested in the Week 6 brief and adds variables motivated by the EDA. Feature definitions preserve uncertainty in the source. Measures derived during or after a visit must not be used to predict a pre-visit outcome without a historical, leakage-safe reconstruction.

Interpretation & Feature-Engineering Results¶

  • Age groups: The 5,000 appointment rows are distributed across all five bands. The largest is age 65+ with 1,471 rows (29.4%); ages 0-17 account for 970 (19.4%). The other groups range from 825 to 873 rows. These are appointment counts, not unique-patient counts; the master contains 4,443 distinct patients.
  • High-risk screening indicator: It is positive for 4,125 rows and unknown for 875; there are no zero values. In this source, chronic conditions are recorded as named conditions or Not recorded, with no explicit no-condition group. The 82.5% positive share is therefore the result of the indicator definition and available documentation; it must not be read as the prevalence of clinically high-risk patients. Keep the 875 unknowns distinct and consider separating age 65+ from documented chronic history in later models.
  • Admissions and severity: Of 5,000 appointments, 4,414 (88.3%) have no linked admission; 586 (11.7%) are split into 155 short, 245 medium, and 186 long stays. The severity score covers all rows and is relatively balanced: 1,682 mild (33.6%), 1,696 moderate (33.9%), and 1,622 severe (32.4%). Stay and severity are observed during or after care, so they are not valid pre-visit predictors.
  • Insurance and revenue: All 5,000 rows have a recorded InsuranceID, but active coverage is unverified, so this feature has no variation for an insured/uninsured comparison. Positive bills form four equal-sized quartiles of 1,250 appointments each; no appointment falls into the No bill group.
  • Satisfaction: A numeric appointment rating is available for 1,756 rows (35.1%); 3,244 (64.9%) remain Not rated. Among rated rows, 719 are Low (41.0%), 387 Moderate (22.0%), 346 High (19.7%), and 304 Very high (17.3%). The limited response coverage means the rating profile may not represent all patients.
  • Facility and department measures: The facility score and workload index are mapped to all 5,000 appointment rows. The former is a facility-level average based on feedback, while the latter is a department percentile based on listed staff, not actual shift workload. Part 3's facility mapping mismatch limits facility attribution.
  • Payment features: The collection ratio and status-conflict flag make payment reconciliation visible for subsequent analysis. Because a transaction can exceed its bill and source status labels conflict with payments, these values describe data records and should be reviewed before finance uses them as performance indicators.

This dictionary documents feature definition, grain, and timing so future models can avoid target leakage and distinguish measured values from proxies.

Interpretation & Feature Dictionary¶

The dictionary contains the ten requested engineered variables plus prior-visit history and two financial quality indicators. The coverage table shows that most derived fields are populated for all 5,000 appointment rows. The meaningful exceptions are the high-risk marker, which has 4,125 positive values and 875 unknowns with no confirmed low-risk cases, and the numeric satisfaction score, available for only 1,756 appointments. The satisfaction category retains all 3,244 missing-feedback appointments as Not rated rather than imputing a score.

The table also clarifies timing: prior appointment count is the clearest chronology-safe feature. Stay duration, disease severity, billed revenue, satisfaction, payment ratio, and same-period facility/workload aggregates are measured during or after the encounter. They describe the cohort but would leak information into a pre-visit model unless rebuilt from earlier periods. Insurance-ID presence is constant in this extract and is not a measure of active coverage.

Interpretation of correlations and heatmap. Four of the five requested pairwise relationships are close to zero in this extract. Age and admission at the first observed encounter have a point-biserial coefficient of 0.0255 (p = 0.0893; n = 4,443). Age and first-visit billed amount have Spearman ρ = -0.0067 (p = 0.6568). Among 578 admitted patients, diagnosis severity and stay duration have ρ = -0.0169 (p = 0.6843). Across 200 departments, workload index and mean satisfaction have ρ = -0.0245 (p = 0.7310). These results do not show meaningful monotonic or linear associations in the selected samples.

The exception is monthly linked receipts versus distinct patient volume: Spearman ρ = 0.9161 (p < 0.001; n = 12 months). Higher-volume months tended to have higher recorded receipts. This is a strong association over only one year of observations, not evidence of causation or a validated forecasting relationship.

The heatmap confirms the strongest pair is billed amount versus recorded payments (ρ = 0.91). Billed amount is also moderately associated with claim amount (ρ = 0.46), and payments with claim amount (ρ = 0.42). All other displayed pairs are close to zero (absolute ρ no greater than 0.05 at the shown precision). The financial fields are linked parts of the same billing process, so their associations are expected and do not imply that claims cause payment. Insurance utilization cannot be compared across coverage groups: all 4,443 patients have an InsuranceID recorded, covering 5,000 appointments, and active coverage status is unavailable. The heatmap is descriptive and combines variables at different analytical grains.

Interpretation & Statistical Conclusions. The five primary tests use α = 0.05 and Holm-adjusted p-values. The final decision is based on the adjusted value, while the raw p-value and effect size help show the strength and practical scale of each result.

  • Satisfaction across facilities: Kruskal-Wallis gives H = 14.931, raw p = 0.72695, and adjusted p = 1.000 across 1,675 first-rated patient encounters and 20 facilities. Epsilon-squared is approximately 0. The test does not detect different rating distributions. Facility-level interpretation is additionally limited by the 94.9% DepartmentID/FacilityID mismatch found in Part 3
  • Admission by age group: The chi-square statistic is 9.752 with 4 degrees of freedom (p = 0.04482; adjusted p = 0.17927; n = 4,443). Rates range from 9.6% in ages 35-49 to 13.8% in ages 50-64; the other groups are 10.0%, 11.6%, and 12.4%. Cramer's V = 0.0469 indicates a very small association. Although the unadjusted p-value is below 0.05, the result does not survive Holm correction, so the adjusted decision is to fail to reject independence
  • Severity and stay duration: Among 578 admitted patients, Spearman ρ = -0.01695 (p = 0.68432; adjusted p = 1.000). The estimated relationship is negligible and not statistically significant
  • Department workload and satisfaction: Across 200 departments, ρ = -0.02446 (p = 0.73102; adjusted p = 1.000). This provides no evidence of a monotonic association in the department-level data; workload is only a roster proxy
  • Monthly receipts and patient volume: Across 12 monthly observations, ρ = 0.91608 (p = 0.00003; adjusted p = 0.00014). This is the only test that rejects H0 after correction. Months with more distinct patients tended to have higher receipts, but the short series and shared billing process prevent causal or long-term claims

The insured-versus-uninsured billing test remains unestimable because active coverage is unknown and no uninsured comparison group is present. A failure to reject H0 is not proof that groups are identical.

6.4 - Statistical Analysis Summary¶

The descriptive table shows a broad patient-age distribution, highly variable financial amounts, and satisfaction centered at 3 among the 1,756 rated appointments. The correlation analyses find near-zero relationships for age, severity/stay, and department workload/satisfaction. The one clear association is monthly receipts with patient volume (ρ = 0.916 over 12 months). Among the five hypothesis tests, this monthly relationship alone remains significant after Holm correction; age-group admission has a raw p below 0.05 but an adjusted p of 0.179 and a very small effect (Cramer's V = 0.047).

These results are descriptive of the available extract. They are constrained by the 35.1% feedback coverage, unverified insurance status, billing/payment conflicts, the 94.9% department/facility mapping mismatch, and only 12 monthly observations. Resolve source issues and collect additional periods before treating facility comparisons, financial trends, or monthly associations as operational forecasts.

Part 7: Predictive Analytics, Forecasting & Clustering¶

This part develops baseline forecasts for patient demand and linked financial activity, classification models for admission and patient satisfaction, and clustering analyses for patients, facilities, and departments. The available extract contains one year of appointments, so forecasts are deliberately treated as short-data baselines rather than reliable long-term projections. Predictive features are selected to avoid using direct outcome fields as inputs.

7.1 - Patient Volume, Revenue, and Department Workload Forecasts¶

The assignment requests 12-month forecasts for patient visits, hospital revenue, and department demand. Linked appointment bills and payments are used instead of the unlinked Revenue_Summary table. The code compares a three-month moving-average baseline with Holt’s damped-trend exponential-smoothing model, then uses a rolling one-step backtest on the final three observed months. Annual seasonality is not fitted because only 12 months are available. Department forecasts remain a simple recent-average baseline because each department series is sparse.

Forecasting theory and results. The three-month moving average is a statistical baseline: for every future horizon h it uses the same estimate, $$\hat y_{t+h}=(y_t+y_{t-1}+y_{t-2})/3.$$ It is simple to interpret, but assumes neither trend nor seasonality. For the 200 department series, monthly records are sparse, so the same recent-average method is used as a planning baseline.

Holt's damped-trend exponential smoothing is the statistical forecasting model used for the overall monthly series. It updates an estimated level L and trend T from each new observation y. The level gives weight α to the newest value, while the trend uses β to update its slope; φ dampens that slope in future months:

$$L_t = αy_t + (1-α)(L_{t-1}+φT_{t-1}), \quad T_t = β(L_t-L_{t-1})+(1-β)φT_{t-1}.$$

The forecast is the current level plus a progressively damped trend. The code uses fixed parameters α = 0.3, β = 0.1, and φ = 0.8; these are transparent modelling choices, not values selected by a large training history. No annual seasonal component is fitted: one year of monthly values is not enough to estimate a repeating yearly pattern reliably.

The backtest makes rolling one-month-ahead predictions for the final three observed months, using only earlier months at each step. MAE is the mean absolute forecast error; RMSE gives more weight to large errors. Lower values are preferable, but three test months are far too few to establish reliable model superiority, and this backtest does not validate a 12-month horizon.

On this short backtest, the three-month mean has lower errors for all three measures. For patient visits, MAE/RMSE are 6.56/7.98 versus 7.29/9.69 for Holt. For gross billed amount, they are 900,199/967,054 versus 1,600,514/1,824,505 source units. For recorded receipts, they are 1,542,975/1,830,604 versus 1,819,092/2,223,477. The evidence therefore favors the simpler baseline for this limited comparison, not as a proven long-term winner.

The moving-average forecast is 411.67 visits per month, 62.81 million in gross bills, and 56.84 million in recorded receipts. Holt starts at about 411.92 visits, 62.62 million billed, and 56.53 million in receipts in January 2027, then declines gently through the year as its damped trend approaches a stable level. The department baseline ranks DEP115 (Obstetrics & Gynecology) and DEP101 (Emergency) highest at 56 visits each over the next 12 months. These values are scenarios in source units, not commitments. Billed totals are not verified accounting revenue, the currency is unspecified, and billing-status/payment conflicts remain unresolved.

7.2 - Hospital Admission Prediction¶

This model estimates whether an encounter is linked to an admission. It keeps the first observed encounter per patient and uses a stratified 75/25 train/test split. Logistic regression models the log-odds as a weighted combination of input variables, $$\log(p/(1-p))=β_0+β_1x_1+\cdots+β_kx_k,$$ then converts the result to an admission probability between 0 and 1. Numeric features are median-imputed and standardized, while categorical features are mode-imputed and one-hot encoded. Class weighting gives the minority admission class more influence during fitting.

Predictors include demographics, visit type, department, chronic-condition history, prior visits, diagnoses, and severity. Diagnosis and severity are assumed available when supporting an admission decision. Billing, length of stay, feedback, and the admission target are excluded to avoid direct target leakage.

Interpretation of the admission model. The test set contains 1,111 unique patients, of whom 128 (11.5%) had an admission on their first observed encounter. The logistic model reaches 51.5% accuracy, 46.8% balanced accuracy, and ROC AUC 0.466. The admission recall is 40.6%, but precision is only 10.1%: of 515 encounters predicted as admissions, just 52 were actual admissions, while 463 were false positives. It also misses 76 of the 128 actual admissions.

These results do not support using this model for admission decisions. The AUC is below 0.5 and balanced accuracy is below chance-level 0.5; the class-weighted model produces many false alerts without reliably separating admissions. The first-encounter holdout avoids putting the same patient in both sets, but it is a random split rather than a future-time evaluation. More informative clinical and encounter data, a temporal validation set, calibration, and clinical review would be needed before reconsideration. The model is an educational baseline, not a clinical decision tool.

7.3 - Patient Satisfaction Prediction¶

This model predicts one of the five recorded rating classes (1-5) from demographic, clinical, and appointment characteristics. It uses the first rated encounter per patient and a stratified 75/25 train/test split. A multiclass logistic regression estimates a score for each rating class and converts the scores to class probabilities with the softmax function; the most probable class is selected. Numeric inputs are imputed and standardized, while categorical inputs are imputed and one-hot encoded.

The target rating and post-visit financial outcomes are excluded from predictors. This analysis applies only to patients who submitted feedback; the EDA found linked ratings for 1,756 of 5,000 appointments (35.1%).

Accuracy is 20.3% and balanced accuracy is 20.1%, almost the 20% accuracy expected from chance-level guessing across five equally considered classes. Class-level F1 scores range from 0.141 to 0.259, with no rating category predicted reliably.

The available demographic, clinical, and appointment fields do not provide useful out-of-sample rating prediction in this baseline. Feedback is also selective: 35.1% of appointment rows have a linked rating, so respondents may differ from non-respondents. The model should not be used to rank departments, facilities, or staff. Improving response coverage and investigating low ratings directly are more actionable than acting on these predictions.

7.4 - Patient, Facility, and Department Clustering¶

K-means assigns each observation to the nearest centroid and minimizes the total squared distance from observations to their assigned centroids. Since distance depends on measurement scale, the variables are standardized first. The patient analysis compares 2-5 cluster solutions using silhouette score; larger values indicate better separation in this feature space. Facility and department analyses use three clusters for a compact operational profile, so those group counts are descriptive choices rather than an optimized result.

Patient inputs summarize age, chronic-history documentation, appointment frequency, mean severity, and satisfaction; admission count is reported after clustering for profile comparison, not used to form the patient groups. Missing numeric values are median-imputed for the clustering step. Facility and department inputs summarize observed demand, satisfaction, admission rates, billing, and listed staff. Cluster numbers have no intrinsic order or meaning; the profile averages must be read to interpret them.

Interpretation of cluster profiles. The patient silhouette score is highest for k = 3 (0.411), just above k = 2 (0.400); scores are lower for k = 4 (0.302) and k = 5 (0.312). The three groups are moderately separated in the standardized feature space. Their profiles show different data and service patterns:

  • Cluster 0: 1,117 patients (25.1%). No chronic history is recorded for this group. Only 30.4% have a classifiable high-risk proxy, and every classifiable case is flagged because age is 65+. The remaining histories are unknown; this cluster must not be labeled low-risk or universally high-risk
  • Cluster 1: 2,920 patients (65.7%). Chronic history is documented for all patients in this group. They average one observed appointment and 0.116 admissions per patient. The screening proxy is positive, but it reflects documented chronic history and is not a validated clinical risk score
  • Cluster 2: 406 patients (9.1%). This group averages 2.116 appointments and 0.276 admissions per patient; 96.6% have a documented chronic condition. The proxy is classifiable for 98.0% and positive for all those cases. This repeat-use profile may merit continuity-of-care review, but it does not prove clinical high risk or predict future admission.

The facility clusters contain 8, 5, and 7 facilities. Their mean satisfaction values are 2.949, 2.860, and 2.945; appointment volumes average about 261, 225, and 256; admission rates are 10.5%, 12.0%, and 13.1%. These are descriptive profiles, not facility rankings. The 94.9% DepartmentID/FacilityID mismatch may compromise facility assignment.

The department clusters contain 100, 50, and 50 departments. Average satisfaction is 2.961, 2.850, and 2.972, while average appointment volume is 24.91, 24.56, and 25.62. The middle group has three listed nurses on average, compared with four in the first group; actual shifts and workloads are unavailable. These patterns are discussion points for operations teams, not evidence that staffing caused rating differences. Facility and department cluster counts were set to three for compact profiling rather than selected by a validation score.

7.5 - Optional Principal Component Analysis (PCA)¶

PCA creates new, uncorrelated axes from weighted combinations of the standardized patient features; the first axis captures the greatest possible variance and the second captures the greatest remaining variance. The two-axis chart is an exploratory projection, not a replacement for the original variables or a clinical mechanism.

Variance explained by component 1: 33.4%
Variance explained by component 2: 17.3%
Variance explained by the two components: 50.7%

Visual 41. The PCA projection shows how the three exploratory patient clusters separate on the first two components.

Interpretation of PCA. The first component explains 33.4% of standardized feature variance and the second 17.3%, for 50.7% together. The two-dimensional plot therefore omits 49.3% of the variation in the original patient features. Some overlap is expected in this projection; it does not show the full cluster geometry. PCA is a visualization aid, not a prediction model or a clinical explanation.

7.6 - Predictive Modeling Summary¶

The admission classifier performs poorly on its holdout set (ROC AUC 0.466; balanced accuracy 0.468), and the satisfaction classifier is near chance (20.1% balanced accuracy across five ratings). Neither is ready for operational decisions. For overall monthly series, the three-month mean has lower one-step backtest errors than the fixed-parameter Holt damped-trend model for visits, gross bills, and receipts; however, the test uses only three months and does not establish 12-month accuracy. Patient clustering selects three groups by silhouette score. One group is dominated by missing chronic histories, another by documented chronic conditions, and a smaller group combines repeat visits with higher recorded admission frequency. None is a clinical risk label. Revisit the models with longer, temporally separated data and validated source relationships.

Part 8: Business Insights & Strategic Recommendations¶

This section translates the EDA, data validation, and model outputs into management actions. Each recommendation is tied to an observed finding and includes a practical measure for follow-up. Data-quality constraints are treated as part of the business problem because they affect the reliability of facility, financial, and patient-experience comparisons.

8.1 - Operational Challenges and Data Reliability¶

The first priority is to resolve source inconsistencies that limit staffing, facility, and financial decisions. The recommendations below distinguish directly observed evidence from items requiring operational verification.

Evidence-led Operational Priorities¶

Priority Evidence in this analysis Recommended action and follow-up measure
Reconcile location identifiers 4,744 of 5,000 appointments (94.9%) disagree on the facility mapped to their department. Validate the DepartmentID-FacilityID master mapping. Track the share of appointments with a verified mapping before publishing facility comparisons.
Improve patient feedback and service recovery Ratings are linked to 1,756 appointments (35.1%); 719 of these (40.9%) are 1 or 2, and the mean is 2.925/5. Increase response coverage and route low ratings for review. Track response rate, low-rating share, and complaint-closure time.
Complete chronic histories 1,131 of 4,443 patient histories (25.5%) are Not recorded; 1,471 appointment rows involve patients age 65+ (29.4%). The engineered risk marker has no confirmed zero group. Add a structured history review. Track completeness and follow-up for older patients; do not treat the proxy as a validated risk prevalence.
Reconcile bills and transactions 323 bills marked Paid still show a balance; 1,626 marked Pending have linked payments. The transaction-derived outstanding balance is 76,582,119 source units. Reconcile invoice status with payment transactions. Track unreconciled bills, balance aging, and payment-allocation rate.
Plan staffing with better workload data Department workload is only a roster proxy; its 10th and 90th percentiles are 10.5 and 89.175. Listed bed status does not measure occupancy. Combine appointment demand with actual rosters, shifts, bed occupancy, and equipment use. Track forecast error and service coverage by shift.
Assess expansion with access evidence There are 415 referral-linked appointments, but no travel-time or verified service-area measure in this extract. Combine patient origins, referral completion, facility capacity, and travel times before choosing locations or services. Track population within target travel time and referral completion by district.
Improve financial reporting Forecasts use gross bills and linked receipts, not reconciled accounting revenue; currency is unspecified and Revenue_Summary is unlinked. Reconcile the finance sources before setting revenue targets. Track billed totals, receipts, and validated balances separately.

Interpretation. The evidence points first to data reliability: facility comparisons are affected by identifier mismatches, and financial balances are affected by status/transaction conflicts. Patient experience and record completeness are the next actionable areas. Forecasts and clusters can guide questions for managers, but current validation is too limited to justify staffing, expansion, or clinical decisions on their own.

8.2 - High-Risk Groups and Patient Experience¶

The patient profile contains 4,443 distinct people. Chronic conditions are documented for 3,312 (74.5%), while 1,131 histories (25.5%) are Not recorded. The 1,471 appointment rows in the age-65+ band represent 29.4% of the appointment cohort, not 29.4% of distinct patients. In the patient clustering, the 406-person repeat-use group averages 2.116 appointments and 0.276 recorded admissions per patient; this can inform continuity-of-care review, but neither the cluster nor the engineered screening marker is a clinical diagnosis. The first priority is complete, dated health histories and clinician-led review.

Only 35.1% of appointments have linked feedback. Among the 1,756 ratings, 719 (40.9%) are 1 or 2 and the mean is 2.925/5. Increase feedback coverage and investigate low-scoring experiences. Because responses are selective and facility mapping is inconsistent, ratings should not be used as unadjusted facility or staff rankings.

8.3 - Resource Optimization and Revenue Improvement¶

The three-month mean baseline projects about 412 visits, 62.81 million in gross billed amounts, and 56.84 million in recorded receipts per month. In the three-month backtest it has lower MAE than Holt's damped-trend model for all three series, but this short validation cannot establish a reliable annual forecast. Department forecasts put DEP115 (Obstetrics & Gynecology) and DEP101 (Emergency) highest at 56 visits each over the next year; use these values to start a manager review, not to set staffing levels.

The department workload index uses listed staff counts and cannot represent shift coverage. The source bed table marks beds available but contains no occupancy events, so it cannot validate bed utilization. The 76.58 million calculated outstanding balance should be reconciled from transactions; the amount is in unspecified source units, and the unlinked Revenue_Summary cannot confirm recognized revenue. Track gross bills, paid transactions, and validated outstanding amounts separately.

8.4 - Strategic Recommendations and Management Follow-up¶

  1. Repair data lineage. Assign owners and deadlines to validate department/facility mappings and reconcile billing statuses against transactions.
  2. Build a patient-experience feedback loop. Increase response coverage, investigate low ratings, and document service recovery by department after location mappings are verified.
  3. Improve longitudinal patient records. Collect structured chronic-condition history and dated updates; use the current screening proxy only to direct review, not to make clinical decisions.
  4. Use forecasts as rolling planning references. Compare monthly actuals with both the moving-average baseline and Holt model. Reassess once several years of monthly data are available.
  5. Plan staffing from observed capacity. Combine demand with shift rosters, bed occupancy, and equipment utilization before reallocating resources.
  6. Assess expansion using access evidence. Combine geographic demand, referral completion, travel times, and facility capacity before selecting underserved districts or services.
  7. Govern model use responsibly. Neither classification model is ready for operational decisions. Monitor performance across patient groups, validate with future-time data, and keep clinical decisions with qualified clinicians.

These actions focus on source reliability, patient experience, capacity planning, and financial transparency. Clinical, operations, finance, and data teams should review the proposed measures together each month.

The master dataset is the quality-controlled integration output; engineered features retain documented proxy labels and unknown categories where source evidence is incomplete.
